::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
Which biomarker will tell you the drug is working, and how soon after dosing
should you measure it? The answer comes from the target family, not from the
compound.
:::

## 1. Four families

Almost every marketed drug acts on one of four kinds of protein. Knowing which
tells you where the drug must reach, how quickly the effect appears, and how the
system pushes back.

| Family | Where it sits | Drug does what | Effect appears in | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Receptors** | Cell surface, or inside the cell | Mimics or blocks a natural signal | Seconds to hours | Beta-blockers, opioids, antihistamines |
| **Enzymes** | Mostly inside cells; some in plasma | Blocks catalysis | Hours to weeks | Statins, ACE inhibitors, kinase inhibitors |
| **Transporters** | Membranes | Blocks movement of a substance | Minutes to hours | SSRIs, SGLT2 inhibitors, diuretics |
| **Ion channels** | Membranes | Opens or blocks a pore | Milliseconds to seconds | Local anaesthetics, calcium blockers |

## 2. Receptors

A receptor's job is to receive a signal from outside and produce a change
inside. Drugs either imitate the natural signal or prevent it.

**G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs)** are the largest family and the most
drugged. Seven passes through the membrane; something binds outside; the shape
changes; a cascade of signalling begins inside. Adrenaline, histamine, opioids
and many neurotransmitters act here. Signalling is amplified — one bound
receptor activates many downstream molecules — which has a consequence that
surprises newcomers: **maximal effect can arrive well before maximal occupancy**.
The *spare receptor* phenomenon in `P-05` is exactly this.

**Receptor tyrosine kinases** span the membrane and switch on an enzyme on the
inside when something binds outside. Growth factor signalling runs through them,
which makes them central to oncology.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## A receptor is not an on/off switch

The intuitive picture — agonist binds, receptor turns on, every downstream
pathway fires — is known to be wrong, and the correction matters for modelling.
A receptor samples many conformations; an agonist stabilises *some* of them; and
different signalling proteins engage different regions of the protein. So
different agonists at the same receptor can activate different subsets of
pathways. This is **biased agonism**, and Kenakin's review
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.3410/B1-87), free full text) sets out the evidence.

Two consequences worth carrying:

**The minimal unit of control is the agonist–receptor complex, not the
receptor.** Two agonists at one receptor can have their relative potencies
*reverse* between two downstream readouts — the PACAP peptides do exactly that
across cyclic AMP and IP measurements.

**Efficacy is not one number.** Kenakin calls it "pluridimensional": a ligand
can be an agonist for one pathway and an antagonist or inverse agonist for
another. Propranolol is the textbook case — a classic antagonist and inverse
agonist at G-protein-mediated β-adrenoceptor effects, and an *activator* of ERK
signalling.

For a modeller this means the biomarker you choose does not merely measure the
effect — it decides which effect you are measuring. Two teams modelling the same
drug at the same receptor with different readouts can both be right and
disagree.
:::

**Nuclear receptors** are different in a way that matters for timing. They sit
*inside* the cell, and when bound they travel to the nucleus and change which
genes are transcribed. The drug must therefore get inside — ruling out
antibodies — and the effect requires new protein to be made. **Onset takes hours
to days and outlasts the drug.** Corticosteroids work this way. Any PK/PD model
here needs an explicit delay, because plasma concentration and effect are
separated by transcription and translation.

## 3. Enzymes

Enzymes make and break molecules. Block one and its product falls.

The quantitative subtlety is that **effect follows the product, not the enzyme**.
Inhibit the enzyme completely and the existing pool of product still has to be
consumed or degraded before anything changes. If that pool turns over slowly,
full effect lags inhibition by days or weeks — statins reach steady-state LDL
reduction in about a fortnight while inhibiting the enzyme within hours.

This is the *turnover* or *indirect response* structure, and it is the single
most common source of delay between concentration and effect. `S1` models it
explicitly; recognising it here is what stops you fitting a direct-effect model
to something that will never behave like one.

## 4. Transporters

Transporters move substances across membranes. They matter twice over.

**As targets.** SSRIs block the serotonin transporter; SGLT2 inhibitors block
glucose reabsorption in the kidney; diuretics block sodium transporters.

**As obstacles.** The same protein family decides where *your* drug goes. Efflux
transporters in the gut wall pump absorbed drug straight back out; the same
proteins at the blood–brain barrier keep drugs out of the brain; others in liver
and kidney carry drugs into the cells that eliminate them. A drug can fail purely
because a transporter it was never designed to interact with removes it from
where it needs to be.

Transporters also **saturate**. At high concentration the pump is working flat
out and further increases in dose behave differently — a common source of
nonlinear pharmacokinetics, and a reason a model fitted at one dose level can
mispredict at another.

## 5. Ion channels

Channels are gated pores. Open one and ions flood through, changing the cell's
electrical state within milliseconds — the fastest pharmacology there is.

Two consequences. **Effect is essentially instantaneous** relative to
pharmacokinetics, so concentration and effect can be linked directly with no
delay term. And **the heart is full of them**, which is why every drug programme
screens against the hERG potassium channel: blocking it prolongs cardiac
repolarisation and can cause a fatal arrhythmia. hERG is the most famous
off-target in pharmacology and it appears again in `P-16`.

## 6. Reading the timing off the target

The practical payoff of this lesson is a first guess at model structure before
any data exist.

| If the target is | Effect delay comes from | Model structure to expect |
|---|---|---|
| An ion channel | Nothing — it is immediate | Direct effect on concentration |
| A cell-surface receptor | Signalling, usually fast | Direct effect, or a small effect-site delay |
| An enzyme | Turnover of the product pool | Indirect response / turnover |
| A nuclear receptor | Transcription and translation | Turnover with a substantial lag |
| A transporter | Depends what accumulates | Often indirect, sometimes saturable |

A guess, not an answer — but a guess with a mechanism behind it, which is far
better than picking a structure because it fitted.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Failure mode — hysteresis read as noise
Plot effect against concentration for a drug with delayed action and you do not
get a curve. You get a **loop**: at the same concentration, effect is smaller on
the way up than on the way down, because effect is chasing concentration with a
lag. This is hysteresis, and it is a signature, not a defect.

The failure is to treat the loop as scatter and fit a direct concentration–effect
model through the middle of it. That model will fit acceptably, produce a
plausible EC₅₀, and mispredict every regimen with different timing — because the
parameter it estimated is an artefact of the sampling schedule rather than a
property of the drug.

Seeing a loop should send you to the target family and ask *where the delay comes
from*. Then model that.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. A drug fully inhibits its enzyme within an hour, but the clinical biomarker takes two weeks to plateau. Is the drug slow?
No — the biomarker is. Inhibition is immediate; what you are watching is the
downstream pool turning over. The half-life of the *response* is set by the
degradation rate of whatever the enzyme was making, not by the drug's
pharmacokinetics. Practically: measure the enzyme's direct product for target
engagement, expect the clinical marker to lag, and model the delay explicitly
rather than inflating the drug's apparent half-life to accommodate it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Why does an intracellular target rule out an antibody but not a small molecule?
Antibodies are large, water-loving proteins with no route across a lipid
membrane. Small molecules that are modestly lipophilic diffuse across
unassisted. So a target inside the cell — a nuclear receptor, most kinases, most
enzymes — is reachable by small molecules and not by antibodies. It is the
single most consequential fact in early modality choice, and it is knowable
before any chemistry is done.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Why do transporters cause nonlinear pharmacokinetics but passive diffusion usually does not?
Transporters are proteins, and there are a finite number of them. At low
concentrations transport rate rises in proportion to concentration; once the
transporters are saturated the rate plateaus. Passive diffusion has no machinery
to saturate — the rate stays proportional to the gradient at any concentration.
So a transporter-dependent process changes character across the dose range, and
a model fitted at one dose level can mispredict badly at another. This is the
same saturation mathematics as Michaelis–Menten metabolism in `P-09`.
:::

  Pharmacology for target-by-target detail, free and authoritative.

*Seen in the wild:* a team modelled a nuclear-receptor agonist with a direct
effect model because the fit was good in a single-dose study. The regimen
prediction for chronic dosing was wrong by a wide margin, because the model had
no way to represent an effect that builds over days and persists after drug is
gone. The target family said so on day one.
